https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crmr.text: Image source, Getty Images By Hafsa Khalil ,Â Brandon Drenon Â and Â Ben Rich ,Â lead weather presenter Published 15 August 2026 Updated 28 minutes ago Hawaii is facing flash floods and mudslides that have swept away some homes after category one Hurricane Lala skirted Big Island, leaving one person dead in a car accident. A search-and-rescue operation was under way after several properties were uprooted from their foundations in the coastal communities of Naalehu and Waiohinu. Despite not even making landfall, the storm still dumped up to 35in (89cm) of rain in places, sending torrents raging down mountainsides. More than 200,000 householders were without power. Lala's eyewall howled past the Pacific US state overnight before weakening to a tropical storm, and it is now moving westward, south of Hawaii. The storm came within 30 miles (48km) of Big Island's South Point, but it was close enough to bring flash flooding, Hawaii County said on Sunday. After gaining hurricane strength on Saturday afternoon, packing wind speeds of 91mph, Lala's winds have now weakened to near 65mph, said the National Hurricane Center (NHC) in its latest advisory at 14:00 EDT (18:00 GMT) on Sunday. But the danger is not yet over. Figure caption, "It's actually hard for us to see... I've got a lot of water in my eyes," says a local reporter during a live TV broadcast on the Hawaii County coast Tropical storm warnings remain in effect for all eight of Hawaii's major islands. "Lala is expected to produce additional rainfall of 4 to 8 inches across the Big Island and windward Maui, with maximum storm totals of 30 to 35 inches," the NHC said, while the rest of the island chain can expect rainfall of 4 to 6in. The US National Weather Service's office in Honolulu said it had had reports of two homes being swept away amid the intense rainfall. Mayor Kimo Alameda said the county's civil defence agency had launched a search-and-rescue operation to find people whose homes may have been destroyed in the floods. "What makes this very challenging is that there's rushing water, there's debris, there's boulders on the road, and it's dark," he said earlier. Figure caption, Watch: Strong winds and downpours in Maui and Honolulu as storm Lala approaches About 180 Hawaii National Guard members have been deployed to help with the emergency response. Some 219,000 customers had lost electricity on Hawaii as of Sunday morning local time, according to tracker PowerOutage. Three hospitals also lost power, but had backup generators. Big Island's two main airports, Hilo International and Ellison Onizuka Kona, were temporarily closed, but have since reopened. According to the governor, 190 flights have been postponed. In Maui, some residents were left without water supply on Saturday. Image source, Getty Images Iniki, a powerful category four storm, was the last hurricane to hit Hawaii back in 1992. It caused six deaths and $3bn in damage after making landfall on the southern coast of Kauai. Hurricane season in the US has been relatively quiet the last few years - the last major storm was category three Hurricane Milton, which hit Florida in October 2024. This year has seen a strong El NiÃ±o - a periodically occurring area of unusually warm surface water - develop in the Pacific, driven in part by climate change. As hurricanes and typhoons feed off warm sea waters, this spike in ocean temperatures could facilitate a higher number of storms that grow to have a greater intensity. https://www.politico.eu/article/august-d.text: BRUSSELS — August was the joint-hottest month on record globally, official EU data finds, highlighting the worsening effects of global warming. Average temperatures worldwide temporarily soared to 1.65 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels last month, according to Copernicus, the Earth observation unit of the EU's space program. The only other time monthly global temperatures hit that level was in July 2023. Advertisement Advertisement Copernicus said the record temperatures were "due to global heating from burning fossil fuels," combined with rising sea surface temperatures in the Pacific linked to a strong El Niño climate pattern. "Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which carried out the research for Copernicus. The sweltering August capped a record-breaking European summer of heatwaves, wildfires and droughts, as planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions around the world continue to rise . Global greenhouse gas emissions from human activities last year rose 0.7% to reach a record 54 billion tons of CO2 equivalent, the European Commission said Monday — an annual rate that would likely lock in 1.5 degrees of warming by the end of the decade. The United States led the upward trend, increasing its climate pollution by 2.2% in 2025. In China, the world's top climate polluter, emissions rose 0.1% in 2025, while in India they fell 0.2%. The EU's emissions also fell by 0.2% in 2025, the Commission said. Advertisement Advertisement Sea and air Copernicus' overall figures combine global air and sea surface temperatures. Global surface air temperatures in August hit 16.96C, the joint-hottest monthly temperature ever recorded and surpassing the 30-year average between 1990 and 2020 by 0.85C. The average sea surface temperature was at 21.07C, also the joint-hottest on record. In Europe, August was the fourth-hottest on record, at 1.1C above the 30-year average. Overall, 2026 was Europe's third-hottest summer on record, and the hottest ever recorded in Western Europe.

https://www.runcornandwidnesworld.co.uk/.text: Slovakia Entertainment Leisure Widnes Widnes man builds online following sharing life in Slovakia By Tabitha Wilson Reporter Share 0 Comments 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A WIDNES man who swapped Cheshire for Slovakia nearly three decades ago is building an online following by sharing humorous insights into the differences between life in the two countries. James Blore, who grew up in Widnes before studying at Oxford University, moved to Slovakia in 1998 with plans to combine his passion for teaching and travelling. Nearly 28 years later, he is still there, running a successful language school in the country's second-largest city while attracting thousands of viewers on YouTube. His channel, which has more than 3,000 subscribers, explores everything from Slovak traditions and food to cultural quirks and everyday life, often comparing them with his experiences growing up in the UK. After studying chemistry at university and training as a secondary school science teacher, he realised traditional classroom teaching was not quite for him. “I quite liked the idea of teaching, but I wasn't very good at telling 16-year-olds what to do,” he laughed. After spending time supply teaching and travelling in the United States and Mexico, James decided to retrain as an English language teacher. He then spent a year teaching in Oxford before applying for jobs across what was then widely known as Eastern Europe. Offers soon arrived from Warsaw, Prague and the Slovak town of Humenné. While many people might have chosen one of the bigger cities, James deliberately opted for the smaller destination. “I wanted to go somewhere authentic,” he said. “I felt that if I went to Prague, I would spend my time with lots of English and American people. “Going to Humenné wasn't like that at all. “I spent time with the people who lived there and it was a really good experience.” What was initially intended as a temporary adventure soon became something much bigger. After a couple of years in Humenné, James moved to Košice, where he worked for the British Council before opening his own language school with his wife, whom he met in Slovakia. The business is celebrating its 20th anniversary this year. He said living abroad helped him create a life that suited him better than the one he imagined having in Britain. “I always felt a bit of an outsider in the UK,” he said. “Coming to Slovakia put me in a position where being different was expected, and suddenly that became much more comfortable. “In Britain, you are expected to fit in. “In Slovakia I was expected not to fit in, and that was fine.” James enjoys Slovakian cuisine (Image: The School of Blore) As well as enjoying a successful teaching career, James has recently found a new audience online. His YouTube channel began last year after he decided to put video editing and presentation skills he had developed through a niche board game podcast to use in a new way. The videos cover topics ranging from cultural misunderstandings and language differences to everyday observations about Slovak life. When asked about the biggest differences between the two countries, he pointed to the slower pace of life, access to the countryside, and what he sees as a less processed food culture. “The countryside is beautiful and less crowded,” he said. James is a keen birder and says there are an amazing number of birds that you wouldn’t see in the UK. James is an avid birder (Image: The School of Blore) For those considering a visit, James believes Slovakia remains one of Europe's most underrated destinations. While many travellers head straight to the capital Bratislava, he recommends exploring further afield. The High Tatras mountains, historic towns and extensive countryside are among his highlights, while birdwatching has become one of his favourite hobbies since moving there. “There are loads of lovely places and lots of beautiful countryside,” he said. “I think people would be surprised by Slovakia. “It’s not some backwater, Borat kind of place.” James' YouTube channel can be found at @bloresk , where he regularly posts videos about life in Slovakia, British and Slovak culture, and the realities of living abroad after nearly three decades away from his Widnes roots.
